explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Peter says he is "…a witness of Christ’s sufferings…" (1 Peter 5:1). He isn't talking about suffering from far away, either. He writes to people in a hard season as someone who saw Christ's sufferings. He also adds that he's a partaker of the glory to be revealed, so the suffering isn't the end of his sentence.

Peter says the opposite, friend. He calls himself "…a witness of Christ’s sufferings…" (1 Peter 5:1). So the card's statement is true, and the verse says it plainly. He's writing to people in a hard season, and he points to what he witnessed. I think that gives his words real weight.

That's the picture, friend. Peter says, "Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you…" (1 Peter 5:2). A shepherd watches over the sheep. He doesn't just stand there and point at them. And notice that the flock is God's, so the elders are looking after something that belongs to Him.

Builders is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the picture Peter uses here. He says, "Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you…" (1 Peter 5:2). A shepherd's work is watching over sheep, so the elders are to watch over people. And the flock is God's, so they're looking after something that belongs to Him.

A field is a good guess, friend, but it's not the picture Peter uses here. He says, "Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you…" (1 Peter 5:2). Shepherds watch over sheep, and that's the job he hands the elders. The flock belongs to God.

Not quite, friend. Peter says to watch over the flock "not out of greed, but out of eagerness…" (1 Peter 5:2). Greed is the very thing he rules out. The elders are to serve eagerly, not with one eye on what they can get.

Right, friend. Peter says the elders are to watch over the flock "not out of greed, but out of eagerness…" (1 Peter 5:2). Greed is what he rules out. He wants them eager to serve, and I think that's a much better motive than chasing a payday.

That's it, friend. Peter says, "not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock." (1 Peter 5:3). Lording it over people means throwing your weight around. An example is the opposite, because people can look at how the elders live and see the way. I think that's a much kinder way to lead.

Teaching is good work, friend, but that's not the word Peter uses here. He says, "not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock." (1 Peter 5:3). An example is something people can see. The elders show the way by how they live.

Friendship is a lovely thing, friend, but it's not the word Peter picks. He says, "not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock." (1 Peter 5:3). The elders are to show the way by how they live, instead of throwing their weight around.

Other way around, friend. Peter says the elders "…will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away." (1 Peter 5:4). So this crown doesn't fade, ever. It comes when the Chief Shepherd appears. I'd call that a crown worth waiting for.

That's right, friend. Peter says the crown of glory "…will never fade away." (1 Peter 5:4). He says it will come when the Chief Shepherd appears. I can't say that about anything I've ever pulled out of an oven.

Yes, friend. Peter says, "Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders." (1 Peter 5:5). The elders are told to be examples, and the young men are told to submit. Each group gets its own job.

That's flipped, friend. Peter says, "Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders." (1 Peter 5:5). The word is submit, not lead. The elders were just told to be examples, and now the young men get their own instruction.
Not this time, friend. Peter says, "Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders." (1 Peter 5:5). That's the instruction, plain and simple. Correcting isn't the word he uses.

That's the word, friend. Peter quotes, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." (1 Peter 5:5). Notice the two sides of it: grace goes to the humble, and opposition goes to the proud. I'd rather be on the grace side.

Not quite, friend. The line reads, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." (1 Peter 5:5). Peter never says God opposes the weak. The word is proud, and that's the one that goes in the blank.
Close enough to tempt you, friend, but no. The line reads, "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." (1 Peter 5:5). Lazy isn't in it. The word is proud, and humble is its opposite.
Yes, friend. Peter says, "Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you." (1 Peter 5:7). He gives the reason right there in the verse: He cares for you. So you can hand the worry over.
It's true, friend. Peter says, "Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you." (1 Peter 5:7). He even gives the reason. God cares for you.

That's what Peter says, friend. He calls the devil your adversary, and says he is "…seeking someone to devour." (1 Peter 5:8). That's no friendly visit. Peter wants his readers watchful because the danger is real.

Not following, friend. Peter says the adversary prowls around like a roaring lion, "…seeking someone to devour." (1 Peter 5:8). That's why he says to be sober-minded and alert. He's not a pal looking for a buddy.

Nope, friend. Peter says the adversary the devil is "…seeking someone to devour." (1 Peter 5:8). He's compared to a lion on the prowl, not to someone looking for a place to hide. That's why Peter calls his readers to be watchful.
That's it, friend. Peter says, "Resist him, standing firm in your faith…" (1 Peter 5:9). He doesn't tell them to run or to bargain. He tells them to stand, and to stand in their faith.
Peter doesn't say that, friend. He says, "Resist him, standing firm in your faith…" (1 Peter 5:9). Hiding isn't in the verse. The word is stand.
Not a chance, friend. Peter says, "Resist him, standing firm in your faith…" (1 Peter 5:9). He never says to make peace with the devil. He says to resist and stand firm.

Yes, friend. Peter says to stand firm "…in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering." (1 Peter 5:9). So his readers aren't facing it alone. Their brothers all over the world are going through the same kinds of suffering. That's worth knowing when a trial feels lonely.

It's true, friend. Peter says to stand firm "…in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering." (1 Peter 5:9). They aren't the only ones in it. Their brothers throughout the world are in it too.

That's right, friend. Peter says the God of all grace "…will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you." (1 Peter 5:10). Four promises in one verse. And notice the word Himself: God does it personally.

That's not in the verse, friend. Peter says the God of all grace "…will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you." (1 Peter 5:10). He doesn't promise an explanation. He promises that God will do the work Himself.

That's not what Peter says, friend. He says the God of all grace "…will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you." (1 Peter 5:10). The promise is about what God does for them. Repaying enemies isn't in it.

Not quite, friend. Peter says, "…after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace…will Himself restore you…" (1 Peter 5:10). The words are a little while, not a long time. After that, God Himself steps in to restore them. I think that's a phrase worth holding onto.
Right, friend. Peter says, "…after you have suffered for a little while…" God will restore them (1 Peter 5:10). The words are a little while. He doesn't say it will drag on.

That's him, friend. Peter writes, "Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly…" (1 Peter 5:12). Peter calls him a faithful brother. That's a good thing to have on your record.

Timothy is a good name, friend, but it isn't the one Peter gives here. He writes, "Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly…" (1 Peter 5:12). Silvanus is the man he calls a faithful brother. The letter was written through him.

Tychicus is a good guess, friend, but it isn't the name in this verse. Peter writes, "Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly…" (1 Peter 5:12). Silvanus is the one Peter regards as a faithful brother. Peter also says he wrote to encourage them and to testify that this is the true grace of God.
